questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 68-year-old male presents with a 3-day history of productive cough, rust-colored sputum, and high fever. On examination, he appears disoriented to time and place. His vitals show a temperature of 39°C, respiratory rate of 32/min, and blood pressure of 86/50 mmHg. Laboratory investigations reveal a serum urea level of 9.2 mmol/L. Based on the CURB-65 scoring matrix, what is the most appropriate management disposition for this patient?[cite: 13]

options.A: Outpatient management with oral Amoxicillin therapy
options.B: Home-based isolation with tele-health monitoring every 48 hours
options.C: Inpatient hospital admission for empirical intravenous antibiotic therapy
options.D: Outpatient administration of a single dose of intramuscular Ceftriaxone

questions.explanation: The patient has community-acquired pneumonia. Calculating his CURB-65 score: 1 point for Confusion (disoriented), 1 point for elevated Urea (>7 mmol/L), 1 point for Respiratory rate (≥30), and 1 point for Age (≥65). Total score = 4. A CURB-65 score of 3 or greater indicates severe pneumonia that necessitates inpatient hospital admission and close monitoring for potential ICU escalation[cite: 13].

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 22-year-old tall, thin male is brought to the resuscitation bay after experiencing sudden-onset, severe right-sided pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness while lifting weights. On physical examination, he is in respiratory distress, cyanotic, and tachycardic (124 bpm) with a blood pressure of 82/48 mmHg. Tracheal deviation to the left side is noted alongside absent breath sounds over the entire right hemithorax. What is the immediate next step in managing this patient?[cite: 13]

options.A: Obtain an immediate bedside expiratory erect chest X-ray
options.B: Perform immediate needle decompression at the 2nd intercostal space in the midclavicular line
options.C: Arrange for an urgent high-resolution contrast-enhanced CT scan of the chest
options.D: Initiate non-invasive continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) ventilation

questions.explanation: This patient presents with classic signs of a life-threatening tension pneumothorax (hypotension, tachycardia, tracheal deviation, absent breath sounds). It is an absolute emergency and a clinical diagnosis; management cannot be delayed for radiologic confirmation. The immediate next step is needle decompression (traditionally at the 2nd intercostal space, midclavicular line) to convert it into an open pneumothorax, followed by a formal tube thoracostomy[cite: 13].

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 34-year-old female with a long-standing history of difficult-to-control asthma presents with recurrent episodes of wheezing, low-grade fever, and the expectoration of thick, brownish mucus plugs. Laboratory testing shows a peripheral blood eosinophil count of 1,200/μL and a significantly elevated total serum IgE level of 1,850 IU/mL. A high-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) scan of the chest shows proximal, central bronchiectasis. Which of the following immunopathological profiles is most characteristically associated with this condition?[cite: 13]

options.A: Isolated Type I hypersensitivity response to Aspergillus spores
options.B: A combined Type I and Type III hypersensitivity reaction causing central bronchiectasis
options.C: Isolated Type IV cell-mediated hypersensitivity causing non-caseating granulomas
options.D: Type II cytotoxic antibody-mediated damage targeted against the basement membrane

questions.explanation: The clinical presentation meets the Rosenberg-Patterson criteria for Allergic Bronchopulmonary Aspergillosis (ABPA), classically seen in asthmatics and cystic fibrosis patients. The condition is driven by a mixed Type I (IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation) and Type III (IgG immune-complex mediated tissue damage) hypersensitivity response to colonized Aspergillus fumigatus antigens, resulting in characteristic central bronchiectasis and eosinophilic inflammation[cite: 13].

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 52-year-old male working at an automotive manufacturing facility presents with progressive, dry cough and exertional dyspnea over the last 9 months. On auscultation, fine end-expiratory velcro crackles are heard at both lung bases. The clinician suspects early-stage interstitial lung disease (ILD). Which of the following objective functional or gas-exchange parameters is the most sensitive indicator for detecting early alveolar-capillary membrane disruption before structural lung volumes drop significantly?[cite: 13]

options.C: Diffusing Capacity of the Lung for Carbon Monoxide (DLCO)

questions.explanation: In early interstitial lung disease (ILD), structural changes and alveolar wall thickening occur before a prominent restrictive pattern drops total lung volumes. Diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide (DLCO) measures gas exchange across the alveolar-capillary membrane and serves as the earliest and most sensitive physiological marker for interstitial or pulmonary vascular diseases[cite: 13].

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 48-year-old obese male ($BMI = 34.5 	ext{ kg/m}^2$) is evaluated for persistent daytime somnolence, morning headaches, and unrefreshing sleep. His wife reports loud, erratic snoring with frequent choking episodes during the night. Vitals reveal a blood pressure of 152/96 mmHg. Polysomnography reveals an Apnea-Hypopnea Index (AHI) of 32 events/hour. Which of the following is the most effective initial long-term therapeutic intervention for this patient?
questions.explanation: An AHI >30 defines severe Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA). The first-line, gold-standard therapy for symptomatic moderate-to-severe OSA is nocturnal continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP). It acts as a pneumatic splint that keeps the upper airway patent during sleep, thereby resolving nocturnal hypoxia, improving daytime hypersomnolence, and reducing long-term cardiovascular risks.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 64-year-old chronic smoker with a 40 pack-year history presents with an acute worsening of his baseline dyspnea, increased sputum volume, and a change in sputum purulence over the last 48 hours. On examination, he has prolonged expiration and diffuse expiratory wheezes. Arterial blood gas shows: $pH = 7.32$, $pCO_2 = 54 	ext{ mmHg}$, $pO_2 = 58 	ext{ mmHg}$. After initiating oxygen via a Venturi mask and nebulized bronchodilators, which intervention is most appropriate next?

options.A: Immediate endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation
options.B: Intravenous loop diuretics and bolus aminophylline
options.C: Non-invasive positive pressure ventilation (NIPPV) and systemic corticosteroids
options.D: High-dose sedatives to control agitation and reduce metabolic demand

questions.explanation: This patient is experiencing a severe acute exacerbation of COPD with respiratory acidosis ($pH < 7.35$, $pCO_2 > 45 	ext{ mmHg}$) and hypoxemia. Non-invasive positive pressure ventilation (NIPPV/BiPAP) is highly effective in this setting; it unloads respiratory muscles, improves alveolar ventilation, lowers $pCO_2$, and significantly reduces the need for endotracheal intubation. Short-course systemic corticosteroids and empirical antibiotics are also indicated.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 60-year-old male presents with slowly progressive exertional dyspnea and a dry, hacking cough for 1 year. He has no significant occupational or environmental exposures. Physical examination reveals prominent digital clubbing and bilateral, late-inspiratory fine velcro crackles. High-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) shows subpleural, basal-predominant reticular opacities with honeycombing and traction bronchiectasis. Which of the following is the standard mechanism-targeted agent used to slow functional decline in this condition?
questions.explanation: The clinical and radiographic presentation is diagnostic of Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis (IPF) demonstrating a Usual Interstitial Pneumonia (UIP) pattern. Immunosuppressive therapy (steroids/azathioprine) is harmful in IPF. Treatment relies on antifibrotic agents such as Nintedanib (a tyrosine kinase inhibitor) or Pirfenidone (TGF-beta inhibitor), which slow the rate of decline in forced vital capacity (FVC).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 42-year-old female undergoes a total abdominal hysterectomy for uterine fibroids. On post-operative day 4, she suddenly develops sharp right-sided chest pain, acute dyspnea, and tachycardia. On examination, her pulse is 112/min, respiratory rate is 26/min, and $SpO_2$ is 89% on room air. Her chest is clear to auscultation. An ECG reveals sinus tachycardia with a transient S1Q3T3 pattern. What is the most appropriate diagnostic imaging study to confirm the suspected diagnosis?

options.C: High-resolution non-contrast CT of the chest
options.D: Duplex ultrasonography of the lower limbs

questions.explanation: The patient has a high clinical probability for an acute pulmonary embolism (post-operative status, sudden onset pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea, tachycardia, hypoxia with a clear chest). Computed Tomographic Pulmonary Angiography (CTPA) is the diagnostic imaging modality of choice/gold standard to confirm a pulmonary embolism in hemodynamically stable patients. Echocardiography is useful for bedside evaluation if the patient is unstable.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 31-year-old female presents with painful, erythematous nodules over her shins (erythema nodosum), bilateral ankle swelling, and low-grade fever. A chest X-ray reveals pronounced symmetrical bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy without lung parenchymal infiltrates. Laboratory workup reveals mild hypercalcemia and elevated serum angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) levels. Transbronchial lung biopsy is performed. Which histopathological feature would confirm this diagnosis?

options.A: Caseating epithelioid granulomas with Langhans giant cells and acid-fast rods
options.B: Non-caseating granulomas containing Schaumann bodies and Asteroid bodies
options.C: Dense alveolar intra-luminal fibrotic plugs (Masson bodies)
options.D: Infiltrative intra-alveolar sheets of atypical CD1a-positive histiocytes

questions.explanation: The presentation represents Löfgren's syndrome, an acute, highly specific presentation of Sarcoidosis. Sarcoidosis is a multisystem disease characterized pathologically by non-caseating epithelioid granulomas. Within these granulomas, laminated calcium-protein structures (Schaumann bodies) and stellate inclusions (Asteroid bodies) are frequently found within multinucleated giant cells. Caseation rules out sarcoidosis and points to tuberculosis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 28-year-old female presents with a 6-month history of worsening exertional syncope and dyspnea. Physical examination reveals an accentuated pulmonic component of the second heart sound (P2), a prominent 'a' wave in the jugular venous pulse, and a parasternal heave. Echocardiography estimates a right ventricular systolic pressure of 65 mmHg without primary valvular or left heart disease. Pulm function tests and CTPA are normal. Right heart catheterization is scheduled. What is the diagnostic hemodynamic threshold for defining pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) during this procedure?

options.A: Mean Pulmonary Artery Pressure (mPAP) $\ge 25 \\text{ mmHg}$ with Pulmonary Capillary Wedge Pressure (PCWP) $> 18 \\text{ mmHg}$
options.B: Mean Pulmonary Artery Pressure (mPAP) $> 20 \\text{ mmHg}$ with Pulmonary Capillary Wedge Pressure (PCWP) $\le 15 \\text{ mmHg}$ and PVR $\ge 2$ Wood Units
options.C: Systolic Pulmonary Artery Pressure $> 40 \\text{ mmHg}$ with normal right ventricular dimensions
options.D: Mean Pulmonary Artery Pressure (mPAP) $> 30 \\text{ mmHg}$ regardless of capillary wedge or vascular resistance vectors

questions.explanation: According to updated clinical consensus guidelines, pre-capillary Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension (PAH/Group 1) is hemodynamically defined during right heart catheterization by a resting Mean Pulmonary Artery Pressure (mPAP) $> 20 \\text{ mmHg}$, a normal left-heart filling pressure (Pulmonary Capillary Wedge Pressure/PCWP $\le 15 \\text{ mmHg}$), and a Pulmonary Vascular Resistance (PVR) $\ge 2$ Wood Units.
